maintainer_vibe: Volunteer moderators who run a high-volume repo (455k stars, 46k forks) through documented policy rather than personal temperament. A GitHub Actions bot enforces initial compliance (PR checklist, conventional commit titles, dedicated branch, issue linkage). When human review kicks in, moderators cite the Contributor Guide or Moderator Handbook directly, are technically specific, and move cases forward quickly. They celebrate compliant contributors with personalized thank-yous and first-PR congratulations, but close low-effort, AI-content, or stale submissions without elaboration.
pr_guidelines: PR titles must use conventional commits format (type scope: description). The bot auto-renames violations and maintainers correct them, as seen on PR #48963 where raisedadead's review focused first on config decisions before any code detail.

The PR description checklist must be completed with real effort, not just tick-boxes. The FAQ states that unchecked or ignored checkboxes signal low effort and the deprioritized label is applied automatically.

Only submit PRs against issues labeled help wanted or first timers only. The FAQ clarifies that issues are not assigned unless you are a long-time contributor and that the first adequate PR to fix an issue is the one that gets merged.
raw_summary: Data drawn from the freeCodeCamp Moderator Handbook, FAQ, and actual PR/issue threads: PR #48963 (tooling update), PR #67087 (accessibility curriculum), PR #66965 (challenge test fix), PR #67079 (CI build failure), issue #62666 (AI-generated PR flood), and forum thread on PR #53199. Moderators are volunteers who triage via a documented handbook: issues are labeled triage-priority, stale issues close after 21 days of inactivity post-feedback, and PRs require two approvals from moderators or dev-team before squash-merge. A GitHub Actions bot gates entry by validating checklist completion, conventional commit titles, and branch isolation. Maintainers use AI tools themselves (Copilot, Claude) for code but the FAQ explicitly states they will not engage with AI-generated comments and responses on issues, PRs, or discussions. The deprioritized label marks low-effort submissions; camper-chan bot sends standard rejection messages without detail. Review tone is technical and direct: raisedadead on PR #48963 explained the npx vs dependency decision and said thanks, tanushriwarhade on PR #67087 said this looks great with one follow-up suggestion, and Jeevankumar-s on PR #67079 flagged a CI failure with an encouraging emoji. Merged PRs get a personal thank-you from the merging moderator and first-time contributors receive explicit congratulations.
maintainer_persona: Policy-bound volunteer moderators. They trust automation for the boring stuff (bot validates checklist, title format, branch rules) so humans can focus on substantive review and technical guidance. They are technically thorough when they engage (raisedadead explained the full npx vs dependency tradeoff), personally warm in approvals (emoji, congratulations, thank-yous), and ruthlessly efficient in rejection (standard bot messages, deprioritized label, casual stale closures). AI-assisted code is welcomed; AI-generated discussion is policy-rejected.
top_dos: Pass the bot gate: use a conventional commit title, complete every checklist item with real context, push from a dedicated feature branch, and link the issue you are fixing
Submit against an issue labeled help wanted or first timers only, and include tests or local verification that you have actually run the CI build
Read the Moderator Handbook and FAQ before opening a PR; maintainers reference these documents constantly and treat guideline compliance as a signal of respect for volunteer time
top_donts: Do not paste AI-generated text into PR descriptions, comments, or issue responses; the FAQ states maintainers will not engage with AI-generated replies
Do not target issues that are not open for contribution or that lack the help wanted label; PRs on closed or unapproved issues get closed immediately
Do not ping maintainers directly or ask for review via @mentions; use the Discord contributors channel or the community forum instead

deep_sections.title: What Contributors Actually Say
deep_sections.body:
Contributor behavior splits into two camps. Compliant contributors follow the flow and get warm reception. On PR #67087, AyushK5ingh added accessibility warning notes and tanushriwarhade replied 'This looks great, thanks for the improvement! I had a small suggestion...' a genuine technical follow-up, not a gatekeeping objection. On PR #66965, AyushK5ingh fixed failing doubly-linked-list tests after a root-cause writeup, and majestic-owl448 merged with 'Thank you for your contribution to the page! We are happy to accept these changes and look forward to future contributions.' The contributor then noted they had already deleted their branch, showing familiarity with fork cleanup.

Non-compliant or AI-assisted contributors get rejected at the gate. On issue #62666, c0d1ng-ma5ter raised a valid concern about AI-slop PRs flooding the repo, but the issue was immediately labeled deprioritized. On PR #67079, Val551 had CI failures and Jeevankumar-s responded with an encouraging 'We would love to be able to merge your changes but it looks like there is an error with the CI build' plus a documentation link, showing the community is helpful when the contributor shows genuine effort to fix issues.

A defensive moment appeared on PR #48963: webpro initially pushed back against raisedadead's request to move knip back to npx, explaining the Node.js 16 engines constraint. The maintainer held firm, webpro relented, revised, and the PR was approved.

deep_sections.title: Hidden Friction Signals
deep_sections.body:
The deprioritized label is the clearest friction signal: it marks PRs as low-effort and signals maintainers will not engage deeply. Issue #62666 was labeled deprioritized within hours of opening, communicating that even well-intentioned meta-concerns about AI floods are not a priority for the volunteer team. The 21-day inactivity rule (from the Handbook) after a maintainer requests changes creates a hard deadline; contributors who do not push updates are silently closed.

The camper-chan bot delivers a standard rejection message: 'This is a standard message notifying you that we have reviewed your pull request and have decided not to merge it. We would welcome future pull requests from you.' with no detail on why. This is used for low-quality or off-scope submissions where the effort to explain is not warranted.

PR #67079 revealed a workflow expectation gap: the contributor did not realize CI was failing until Jeevankumar-s flagged it. The status changed from waiting review to waiting update, and the contributor had to fix e2e timeouts. This shows that PRs touching the client or complex tooling are expected to pass all CI checks before human review begins, and any failure sends the PR back to the author with a status label.

deep_sections.title: Unwritten Rules
deep_sections.body:
Rule one: the checklist is a respect tax. The FAQ says finishing the guidelines carefully earns respect and saves time. The bot auto-applies the deprioritized label when checklists are incomplete or AI text replaces the template. Contributors who pass the bot gate get human attention; those who do not are deprioritized indefinitely. Rule two: two approvals are required, and both must come from moderators or dev-team members. A single thank-you comment does not count; the approval must be a formal GitHub review. Rule three: squash and merge is the only accepted merge strategy, and contributors should not worry about their own commit granularity because the history is squashed. The branch is deleted by the author or the system after merge.

A fourth norm, emerging from the AI discussion: use AI tools for code generation and debugging, but never for the human-facing text. The FAQ draws a bright line: AI in code is fine, AI in comments and responses is not. This extends to PR descriptions: the template must be filled with your own words, even if the code was AI-assisted.

A fifth, technical norm from PR #48963: when a maintainer requests changes that involve a tradeoff (e.g., npx version pinning vs. dependency), respond to the reasoning, not with a counter-argument. Webpro initially pushed back on the Node.js engines constraint but then acknowledged it and revised. The maintainer, raisedadead, stayed technical and said thanks at the end, modeling the expected interaction.
